For an experiment on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$, let
$\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ denote the set of all probability measures
on that measurable space. Its **parametric statistical model** is the parameter
map
$$
\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\qquad \mathsf P(\theta)=P_\theta,
$$
regarded together with its parameter set and sample space
([[def-statistical-experiment]]). The map need not be injective. Unless a
measurable structure on $\Theta$ is supplied separately, no measurability of
$\mathsf P$ is asserted.

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). It is
**dominated** by a supplied positive measure $\mu$ on
$(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ when $\mu$ is sigma-finite
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]) and
$P_\theta\ll\mu$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$
([[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]).
The dominating measure is part of the specified setup. This condition adds no
measurable structure on $\Theta$ and no measurability of
$\theta\mapsto P_\theta$.

Let $\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be a parametric
model, let $\Theta$ be open in $\mathbb R^d$, and let a supplied sigma-finite
measure $\mu$ dominate every $P_\theta$
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]], [[def-dominated-statistical-experiment]]).
Supply as part of the setup a family of nonnegative finite-valued measurable
functions $p_\theta:\mathcal X\to[0,\infty)$ satisfying
$P_\theta(A)=\int_Ap_\theta\,d\mu$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$
([[def-measure-with-density]]). Thus each $p_\theta$ integrates to one.
The density family is supplied, rather than selected from domination alone;
no choice principle, joint measurability in $(\theta,x)$, or common
exceptional null set is asserted. A supplied extended-valued probability
density can be made finite-valued by setting it to zero on its measurable
infinite-value set, which has measure zero because its integral is one.
The QMD condition is unchanged by replacing any supplied density by an
almost-everywhere equal version: for each fixed $h$, the norm in the
condition below changes only on the union of two null sets.
At an interior point $\theta_0$, the model is
**quadratic-mean differentiable (QMD)** with score $s_{\theta_0}$ if
$s_{\theta_0}:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^d$ is measurable,
$\mathbb E_{\theta_0}\|s_{\theta_0}(X)\|^2<\infty$, and
$$
\int\left(\sqrt{p_{\theta_0+h}}-\sqrt{p_{\theta_0}}- \tfrac12 h^Ts_{\theta_0}\sqrt{p_{\theta_0}}\right)^2d\mu=o(\|h\|^2)
$$
as $h\to0$ with $\theta_0+h\in\Theta$. Values of the score on
$\{p_{\theta_0}=0\}$ do not affect this condition. The Fisher information
associated with this QMD score is
$I_{\theta_0}=\mathbb E_{\theta_0}[s_{\theta_0}s_{\theta_0}^T]$; it may be
singular. QMD is an $L^2(\mu)$ condition and does not assert pointwise
differentiability of $p_\theta$ or local mutual absolute continuity of
$P_\theta$ and $P_{\theta_0}$.

For each positive integer $n$, let $(\Omega_n,\mathcal A_n,P_n)$ be a probability space and let $X_n:\Omega_n\to\mathbb R^d$ be measurable into the Borel sigma-algebra generated by the Euclidean open sets, where $d\ge1$ is fixed and $\mathbb R^d$ has the Euclidean norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]], [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]], [[def-probability-measure]]). The spaces and measures may depend on $n$; no common probability space is required.

Write $X_n=o_P(1)$ if for every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$P_n(\|X_n\|_2>\varepsilon)\longrightarrow0.$$
Write $X_n=O_P(1)$, or say that $(X_n)$ is bounded in probability, if for every $\eta>0$ there is $M>0$ such that
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty}P_n(\|X_n\|_2>M)\le\eta.$$
For real-valued variables on one common probability space, $o_P(1)$ is convergence in probability to zero as defined in [[def-convergence-in-probability]].

The norms and tail probabilities are part of the definition. Independence is not implicit in either notation.

Let all random vectors with index $n$ be defined on a common probability space for that $n$; the spaces may vary with $n$. In any fixed finite-dimensional Euclidean space, the following rules hold:

1. If $U_n=o_P(1)$ and $V_n=o_P(1)$, then $U_n+V_n=o_P(1)$. If $U_n=O_P(1)$ and $V_n=O_P(1)$, then $U_n+V_n=O_P(1)$.
2. For positive integers $p,q,r$, let $B:\mathbb R^p\times\mathbb R^q\to\mathbb R^r$ be a fixed map for which there is a constant $C\ge0$ with $\|B(u,v)\|_2\le C\|u\|_2\|v\|_2$ for all $u,v$. Assume in each application that $B(U_n,V_n)$ is a random vector on the same probability space as $U_n,V_n$, for every $n$. If $U_n=o_P(1)$ and $V_n=O_P(1)$, or conversely, then $B(U_n,V_n)=o_P(1)$. If both are $O_P(1)$, then $B(U_n,V_n)=O_P(1)$.
3. If $X_n\Rightarrow X$ in $\mathbb R^d$, then $X_n=O_P(1)$.

The last conclusion is finite-dimensional boundedness in probability. No independence or Axiom of Choice is assumed.

Let $d,k,m\ge1$ be fixed. For each $n$, let $X_n\in\mathbb R^d$ and $Y_n\in\mathbb R^k$ be random vectors on one probability space; the probability space may vary with $n$. Let $X\in\mathbb R^d$ be a random vector on any probability space, and let $c\in\mathbb R^k$ be constant. If $X_n\Rightarrow X$ and $Y_n-c=o_P(1)$, then
$$ (X_n,Y_n)\Rightarrow(X,c). $$
Consequently, for every continuous $h:\mathbb R^{d+k}\to\mathbb R^m$, $h(X_n,Y_n)\Rightarrow h(X,c)$. No independence between $X_n$ and $Y_n$ is required.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be a finite integer. Let $(X_k)_{k\ge1}$ be iid $\mathbb R^d$-valued random vectors with $\mathbb E\|X_1\|^2<\infty$, mean m and covariance Sigma. Then $$n^{-1/2}\sum_{k=1}^n(X_k-m)\Rightarrow N_d(0,\Sigma).$$ The covariance may be singular.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $t>0$. Then
$$\mu(\{f\ge t\})\le\frac1t\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let a dominated finite-dimensional parametric model be quadratic-mean
differentiable, with the supplied density family of [[def-qmd-path]], at an interior point $\theta_0\in\mathbb R^d$, with score
$s_{\theta_0}\in L^2(P_{\theta_0};\mathbb R^d)$. Then
$\mathbb E_{\theta_0}s_{\theta_0}=0$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Write $P_0=P_{\theta_0}$, $S_0=\{p_{\theta_0}>0\}$, and $r_t=\sqrt{p_{\theta_0+t}}-\sqrt{p_{\theta_0}}- \tfrac12t^Ts_{\theta_0}\sqrt{p_{\theta_0}}$. By [F3], $\|r_t\|_{L^2(\mu)}=o(\|t\|)$, and [F12] gives $\mathbb E_0s_{\theta_0}=0$. On $S_0^c$ both $\sqrt{p_{\theta_0}}$ and $s_{\theta_0}\sqrt{p_{\theta_0}}$ vanish, so the probability mass $\alpha_t=\int_{S_0^c}p_{\theta_0+t}\,d\mu$ is $o(\|t\|^2)$. Expanding the QMD approximation in [F3] and applying [F9] to its cross term gives $\|\sqrt{p_{\theta_0+t}}-\sqrt{p_{\theta_0}}\|_2^2= \tfrac14t^TIt+o(\|t\|^2)$.

Normalize the absolutely continuous part on $S_0$ by $q_t=p_{\theta_0+t}\mathbf1_{S_0}/(1-\alpha_t)$, and put $a_t=\sqrt{q_t/p_{\theta_0}}-1$ on $S_0$. Since $\alpha_t=o(\|t\|^2)$, [F3] gives $a_t=\tfrac12t^Ts_{\theta_0}+o_{L^2(P_0)}(\|t\|)$, so $\mathbb E_0a_t^2=\tfrac14t^TIt+o(\|t\|^2)$ and $2\mathbb E_0a_t+\mathbb E_0a_t^2=0$ from $\mathbb E_0(1+a_t)^2=1$. The local envelope makes $f_t=\log(p_{\theta_0+t}/p_{\theta_0})$ square-integrable on $S_0$ and $\|f_t\|_2=O(\|t\|)$. Along every sequence $t\to0$ with $t/\|t\|\to u$, the $L^2$ convergence of $a_t/\|t\|$ has an almost-everywhere convergent subsequence. On it, $2\log(1+a_t)/\|t\|\to u^Ts_{\theta_0}$ pointwise. Since $|f_t|/\|t\|\le L$ and $s_{\theta_0}\in L^2(P_0)$, $|f_t/\|t\|-u^Ts_{\theta_0}|^2\le2L^2+2\|s_{\theta_0}\|^2$; dominated convergence [F10] gives convergence in $L^2$ along that subsequence. Every subsequence has such a subsubsequence, so convergence holds for the full sequence. Sequential compactness of the unit sphere therefore yields $f_t=t^Ts_{\theta_0}+o_{L^2(P_0)}(\|t\|)$. Moreover, the squares $a_t^2/\|t\|^2$ are uniformly integrable because $a_t/\|t\|$ converges in $L^2$ along every convergent direction. Taking the logarithm expansion in expectation requires a tail check. Fix $\varepsilon>0$. On $|a_t|\le\varepsilon$, the Taylor remainder $2\log(1+a_t)-2a_t+a_t^2$ is bounded by $\omega(\varepsilon)a_t^2$, where $\omega(\varepsilon)\to0$. Uniform integrability gives $\mathbb E_0[a_t^2\mathbf1_{|a_t|>\varepsilon}] =o(\|t\|^2)$ and therefore $P_0(|a_t|>\varepsilon)=o(\|t\|^2)$. On this tail, $|2\log(1+a_t)|\le |f_t|+|\log(1-\alpha_t)|$; its expectation is $o(\|t\|^2)$ by the envelope, Cauchy–Schwarz [F9], and the tail probability. The tail expectations of $|a_t|$ and $a_t^2$ are also $o(\|t\|^2)$ by [F9] and uniform integrability. Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ proves that the expected Taylor remainder is $o(\|t\|^2)$. Taking expectations then gives $\mathbb E_0 f_t=2\mathbb E_0a_t-\mathbb E_0a_t^2+o(\|t\|^2) =-\tfrac12t^TIt+o(\|t\|^2);$ the normalization term $\log(1-\alpha_t)$ is $o(\|t\|^2)$.

The squared Hellinger distance $H^2(P_{\theta_0+t},P_0)=\int(\sqrt{p_{\theta_0+t}}-\sqrt{p_{\theta_0}})^2d\mu$ equals $\tfrac14t^TIt+o(\|t\|^2)$ by step 1.1. The affinity $\rho_t=\int\sqrt{p_{\theta_0+t}p_{\theta_0}}d\mu=1-H^2/2$. On $S_0$ let $Y=\sqrt{p_{\theta_0+t}/p_{\theta_0}}$, so $\mathbb E_0Y=\rho_t$. For $y>0$, $\log y\le\log\rho_t+(y-\rho_t)/\rho_t$ follows from $z-1-\log z\ge0$ for $z=y/\rho_t$, since this function has derivative $1-1/z$ and its minimum is $0$ at $z=1$; integrating gives $P_0f_t=2\mathbb E_0\log Y\le2\log\rho_t$. Since $\log(1-x)\le-x$ for $0\le x<1$ because $-x-\log(1-x)$ has derivative $x/(1-x)\ge0$ and value $0$ at $x=0$. Thus $2\log\rho_t\le-H^2$, so for some $c,\delta>0$, $P_0f_t\le-c\|t\|^2$ whenever $\|t\|\le\delta_0$.

Let $\mathbb G_n f=\sqrt n(P_nf-P_0f)$ for the empirical measure $P_n$. The pointwise Lipschitz envelope gives $\|f_t-f_v\|_{L^2(P_0)}\le\|L\|_2\|t-v\|$. The sample and mean processes are continuous in $t$ on compact local balls, so their suprema equal suprema over countable dense subsets and are measurable. To bound the local supremum, take an independent ghost sample $X'_1,\ldots,X'_n$. For each fixed original sample, the supremum of absolute values is convex in the ghost sample vector, so Jensen's inequality replaces $P_0f$ by $n^{-1}\sum_i f(X'_i)$ in the expected supremum. Swapping each pair $(X_i,X'_i)$ with an independent sign and then using the triangle inequality bounds that supremum by twice the expected conditional Rademacher supremum. Condition on the observations for the latter. For the conditional Rademacher process $R_n(f)=n^{-1/2}\sum_i\epsilon_i f(X_i)$, Hoeffding's exponential bound $\mathbb E_\epsilon e^{\lambda(R_n(f)-R_n(g))}= \prod_i\cosh(\lambda(f-g)(X_i)/\sqrt n)\le \exp\{\lambda^2P_n(f-g)^2/2\}$, since $\log\cosh u\le u^2/2$ (integrate $\tanh u\le u$ for $u\ge0$ and use evenness), makes each increment sub-Gaussian with variance proxy $P_n(f-g)^2\le P_nL^2\|t-v\|^2$. Choose successively finer dyadic Euclidean nets of the radius-$r$ parameter ball. At level $k$ the net has at most $(C2^k)^d$ points, each increment from its level-$(k-1)$ parent has scale at most $Cr2^{-k}(P_nL^2)^{1/2}$, and the expected maximum of $N$ centered sub-Gaussian variables of scale $\sigma$ is at most $\sigma\sqrt{2\log(2N)}$, by the exponential-moment bound and optimizing $\lambda$. Summing the resulting bounds uses the convergent series $\sum_{k\ge1}2^{-k}\sqrt{k}$ and gives $\mathbb E_\epsilon\sup_{\|t\|\le r}|R_n(f_t-f_0)|\le C_dr(P_nL^2)^{1/2}$. Symmetrization and $\mathbb E(P_nL^2)^{1/2}\le(P_0L^2)^{1/2}$ therefore give $\mathbb E\sup_{\|t\|\le r}|\mathbb G_n(f_t-f_0)|\le C_d r\|L\|_2.$ For $r_t=f_t-t^Ts_{\theta_0}$, step 2.1 gives $\sup_{\|t\|\le M/\sqrt n}P_0r_t^2=o(n^{-1})$, and increments have the square-integrable pointwise envelope $L+\|s_{\theta_0}\|$. Fix a mesh $\varepsilon>0$ and cover the bounded $h$-ball by finitely many mesh-$\varepsilon$ points. At each center $h_j$, the variance of $\sqrt n\mathbb G_nr_{h_j/\sqrt n}$ is $n\operatorname{Var}_0(r_{h_j/\sqrt n})\le nP_0r_{h_j/\sqrt n}^2=o(1)$, so Chebyshev and finiteness of the net make the maximum over centers $o_P(1)$. For increments within cells, form $g_h=r_{h/\sqrt n}-r_{h_j/\sqrt n}$, where $h_j$ is the center of the cell containing $h$. Each $g_h$ is pointwise bounded by $\varepsilon(L+\|s_{\theta_0}\|)/\sqrt n$. Apply conditional Rademacher chaining to the union of cell classes: at dyadic level $k$ there are at most $C_M\varepsilon^{-d}2^{kd}$ links, each with conditional scale at most $C\varepsilon2^{-k}(P_n(L+\|s_{\theta_0}\|)^2)^{1/2}$ after the $\sqrt n$ normalization. The exponential maximum bound and summation of $\sum_{k\ge0}2^{-k}\sqrt{\log(C_M\varepsilon^{-d})+C_dk}$ give an expected supremum at most $C_M\varepsilon\sqrt{\log(C_M/\varepsilon)}$ after symmetrization and $\mathbb E(P_n(L+\|s_{\theta_0}\|)^2)^{1/2}\le \|L+\|s_{\theta_0}\|\|_2$. Markov's inequality then shows that these cell increments vanish in probability as $\varepsilon\downarrow0$. Letting $n\to\infty$ and then $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ proves $\sup_{\|h\|\le M}|\sqrt n\mathbb G_nr_{h/\sqrt n}|=o_P(1)$. Thus, for each fixed $M$, uniformly over $\|h\|\le M$, $$\ell_n(\theta_0+h/\sqrt n)-\ell_n(\theta_0)=h^T\Delta_n-\tfrac12h^TIh+o_{P_0}(1),\qquad\Delta_n=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^ns_{\theta_0}(X_i).$$ The expectation term is step 2.1; the centered term follows by writing $f_t=t^Ts_{\theta_0}+(f_t-t^Ts_{\theta_0})$ and using the two net bounds.

Reduce $\delta_0$ if needed so the log envelope holds on the radius $2\delta_0$ ball, and put $\delta=\delta_0/2$. Consistency makes $\hat\theta_n$ lie within $\delta$ of $\theta_0$ with probability tending to one. On the dyadic shells $r_j\le\|t\|\le2r_j$ with $r_j=2^jM/\sqrt n$, exact maximization and $\ell_n(\hat\theta_n)\ge\ell_n(\theta_0)$ require $\sqrt n\sup_{\|t\|\le2r_j}|\mathbb G_nf_t|\ge c n r_j^2$. The expectation bound in step 3.1 and Markov's inequality [F11] bound the probability of this event by $C/(\sqrt n r_j)=C/(2^jM)$. Summing the geometric series and then letting $M\to\infty$ proves $\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta_0)=O_{P_0}(1)$ using [F4]. The argument used only consistency, feasibility of $\theta_0$, and the maximizing inequality; it therefore proves the same bound for any exact maximizer over a subset containing $\theta_0$.

Put $\hat h_n=\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta_0)$ and $h_n^*=I^{-1}\Delta_n$. The multivariate CLT [F7] and [F5] make $h_n^*=O_{P_0}(1)$; step 4.1 makes $\hat h_n=O_{P_0}(1)$. For $Q_n(h)=h^T\Delta_n-\tfrac12h^TIh$, $Q_n(h_n^*)-Q_n(h)=\tfrac12(h-h_n^*)^TI(h-h_n^*) \ge\tfrac12\lambda_{\min}(I)\|h-h_n^*\|^2.$ Uniform convergence on bounded balls in step 3.1, feasibility of bounded local $h$ because $\theta_0$ is interior, and exact MLE maximization therefore force $\hat h_n-h_n^*=o_{P_0}(1)$.

Combining this with step 5.1 by [F6] proves both the asymptotic linear representation and the stated normal limit. AC is used only through [F7]–[F8].

$\{p_{\theta_0}=0\}$ do not affect this condition. The Fisher information
associated with this QMD score is
$I_{\theta_0}=\mathbb E_{\theta_0}[s_{\theta_0}s_{\theta_0}^T]$; it may be
singular. QMD is an $L^2(\mu)$ condition and does not assert pointwise
differentiability of $p_\theta$ or local mutual absolute continuity of
$P_\theta$ and $P_{\theta_0}$.

Assume AC for the supplied density representatives in
[[def-score-and-fisher-information]] and [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Let
$X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be iid from a dominated parametric model on an open
$\Theta\subset\mathbb R^d$, and let $\ell_n(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^n\log
p_\theta(X_i)$. For any nested null $\Theta_0\subseteq\Theta$ for which the
maxima exist, the **likelihood-ratio statistic** is
$$L_n=2\left\{\sup_{\theta\in\Theta}\ell_n(\theta)-\sup_{\theta\in\Theta_0}\ell_n(\theta)\right\}.$$

For the Wald and score statistics, specialize to a **regular equality null of
codimension $q$** at an interior point $\theta_0$: this is a null set which,
in a $C^1$ local parameter chart
$\theta=(\psi,\eta)\in\mathbb R^q\times\mathbb R^{d-q}$, is $\psi=0$ near
$\theta_0=(0,\eta_0)$. Its local tangent is the $\eta$-coordinate subspace.
Assume the QMD information $I(\theta_0)$ is positive definite. Let
$\hat\theta_n$ maximize $\ell_n$ over the full parameter space $\Theta$ and
$\tilde\theta_n$ maximize it over the null $\Theta_0$, so the general likelihood-ratio
definition is $L_n=2\{\ell_n(\hat\theta_n)-\ell_n(\tilde\theta_n)\}$.

For the score statistic, assume $\log p_\theta(x)$ is differentiable in the
local chart at the parameter values where it is evaluated, and write
$s_\theta(x)=\nabla_\theta\log p_\theta(x)$. Require explicitly that this
pointwise derivative at $\theta_0$ agrees $P_{\theta_0}$-almost surely with
the QMD score; this compatibility is an assumption, not a consequence of QMD
alone. The pointwise score and its information-matrix convention are those in
[[def-score-and-fisher-information]].

Partition the score and information in $(\psi,\eta)$ coordinates:
$s=(s_\psi,s_\eta)$ and
$$I=\begin{pmatrix}I_{\psi\psi}&I_{\psi\eta}\\I_{\eta\psi}&I_{\eta\eta}\end{pmatrix},\qquad I_{\mathrm{eff}}=I_{\psi\psi}-I_{\psi\eta}I_{\eta\eta}^{-1}I_{\eta\psi}.$$
The matrix $I_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is the information for the tested coordinates
after accounting for the nuisance coordinates. If $d=q$, interpret empty-block
products as zero, so $I_{\mathrm{eff}}=I_{\psi\psi}=I$ and $C$ below is the
empty $q\times0$ matrix. If $d>q$, then $I_{\eta\eta}$ is positive definite;
for $z\ne0$, the quadratic form of $I$ at
$(z,-I_{\eta\eta}^{-1}I_{\eta\psi}z)$ equals
$z^TI_{\mathrm{eff}}z>0$. Thus $I_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is positive definite in
either case. Put
$$
U_n(\theta)=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^n s_\theta(X_i).
$$
For a consistent estimator $\widehat I_{\mathrm{eff},n}$ of
$I_{\mathrm{eff}}$ and a consistent estimator $\widehat C_n$ of
$C=I_{\psi\eta}I_{\eta\eta}^{-1}$, set
$U_{\mathrm{eff},n}=U_{\psi,n}(\tilde\theta_n)-
\widehat C_nU_{\eta,n}(\tilde\theta_n)$. The **score statistic** is
$S_n=U_{\mathrm{eff},n}^T\widehat I_{\mathrm{eff},n}^{-1}U_{\mathrm{eff},n}$.
For a consistent covariance estimator $\widehat V_{\psi,n}$ of the
$\psi$-block of $I^{-1}$, the **Wald statistic** is
$W_n=n\hat\psi_n^T\widehat V_{\psi,n}^{-1}\hat\psi_n$, where
$\hat\psi_n$ is the tested coordinate of $\hat\theta_n$. When a displayed
inverse does not exist, set that statistic to zero; under the regularity
conditions used in the later calibration theorem, the inverse exists with
probability tending to one. This definition gives the statistics and their
normalizations; it asserts no finite-sample or asymptotic distribution.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $X_1,X_2,\ldots$ be iid with law
$P_{\theta_0}$ in a dominated parametric model
$\{P_\theta:\theta\in\Theta\}$, where $\Theta$ is open in $\mathbb R^d$,
$d\ge1$, and $\theta_0\in\Theta$. Let $p_\theta$ be densities with respect
to one supplied sigma-finite measure. Suppose the model is QMD at $\theta_0$
with score $s_{\theta_0}$ and positive-definite information
$I=\mathbb E_{\theta_0}[s_{\theta_0}s_{\theta_0}^T]$. Assume there are a
neighborhood $V$ of $\theta_0$ and a nonnegative measurable $L$ with
$\mathbb E_{\theta_0}L^2<\infty$ such that, on one $P_{\theta_0}$-full set,
$$
|\log p_{\theta_1}(x)-\log p_{\theta_2}(x)|\le L(x)\|\theta_1-\theta_2\| \qquad(\theta_1,\theta_2\in V).
$$
Suppose a measurable exact MLE $\hat\theta_n$ exists and is consistent, in
the sense that $P_{\theta_0}(\|\hat\theta_n-\theta_0\|>\varepsilon)\to0$
for every $\varepsilon>0$. Then
$$\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta_0)=I^{-1}\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^n s_{\theta_0}(X_i)+o_{P_{\theta_0}}(1)\ \Rightarrow\ N_d(0,I^{-1}).$$
Under the same local hypotheses, every consistent measurable exact likelihood
maximizer over a possibly $n$-dependent subset that contains $\theta_0$ is
also root-$n$ bounded in probability.
The conclusion is asymptotic; it gives no exact finite-sample normal law.

For each positive integer $n$, let $(\Omega_n,\mathcal A_n,P_n)$ be a probability space and let $X_n:\Omega_n\to\mathbb R^d$ be measurable into the Borel sigma-algebra generated by the Euclidean open sets, where $d\ge1$ is fixed and $\mathbb R^d$ has the Euclidean norm $\|\cdot\|_2$ ([[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]], [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]], [[def-probability-measure]]). The spaces and measures may depend on $n$; no common probability space is required.

Write $X_n=o_P(1)$ if for every $\varepsilon>0$,
$$P_n(\|X_n\|_2>\varepsilon)\longrightarrow0.$$
Write $X_n=O_P(1)$, or say that $(X_n)$ is bounded in probability, if for every $\eta>0$ there is $M>0$ such that
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty}P_n(\|X_n\|_2>M)\le\eta.$$
For real-valued variables on one common probability space, $o_P(1)$ is convergence in probability to zero as defined in [[def-convergence-in-probability]].

The norms and tail probabilities are part of the definition. Independence is not implicit in either notation.

Let all random vectors with index $n$ be defined on a common probability space for that $n$; the spaces may vary with $n$. In any fixed finite-dimensional Euclidean space, the following rules hold:

1. If $U_n=o_P(1)$ and $V_n=o_P(1)$, then $U_n+V_n=o_P(1)$. If $U_n=O_P(1)$ and $V_n=O_P(1)$, then $U_n+V_n=O_P(1)$.
2. For positive integers $p,q,r$, let $B:\mathbb R^p\times\mathbb R^q\to\mathbb R^r$ be a fixed map for which there is a constant $C\ge0$ with $\|B(u,v)\|_2\le C\|u\|_2\|v\|_2$ for all $u,v$. Assume in each application that $B(U_n,V_n)$ is a random vector on the same probability space as $U_n,V_n$, for every $n$. If $U_n=o_P(1)$ and $V_n=O_P(1)$, or conversely, then $B(U_n,V_n)=o_P(1)$. If both are $O_P(1)$, then $B(U_n,V_n)=O_P(1)$.
3. If $X_n\Rightarrow X$ in $\mathbb R^d$, then $X_n=O_P(1)$.

The last conclusion is finite-dimensional boundedness in probability. No independence or Axiom of Choice is assumed.

Let $d,k,m\ge1$ be fixed. For each $n$, let $X_n\in\mathbb R^d$ and $Y_n\in\mathbb R^k$ be random vectors on one probability space; the probability space may vary with $n$. Let $X\in\mathbb R^d$ be a random vector on any probability space, and let $c\in\mathbb R^k$ be constant. If $X_n\Rightarrow X$ and $Y_n-c=o_P(1)$, then
$$ (X_n,Y_n)\Rightarrow(X,c). $$
Consequently, for every continuous $h:\mathbb R^{d+k}\to\mathbb R^m$, $h(X_n,Y_n)\Rightarrow h(X,c)$. No independence between $X_n$ and $Y_n$ is required.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be a finite integer. Let $(X_k)_{k\ge1}$ be iid $\mathbb R^d$-valued random vectors with $\mathbb E\|X_1\|^2<\infty$, mean m and covariance Sigma. Then $$n^{-1/2}\sum_{k=1}^n(X_k-m)\Rightarrow N_d(0,\Sigma).$$ The covariance may be singular.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. For an integer $k\ge1$, let $G=(G_1,\ldots,G_k)$ have law $N_k(0,I_k)$, so its coordinates are independent $N(0,1)$ random variables. The **chi-square law with $k$ degrees of freedom**, denoted $\chi_k^2$, is the law of
$$
Q_k=\sum_{j=1}^k G_j^2=\|G\|^2.
$$
For $k=0$, define $\chi_0^2=\delta_0$, the point mass at zero. This zero-degree law records a rank-zero projection only; it is not used as a denominator in a Student or Fisher ratio. The multivariate-normal characteristic-function theorem makes the definition independent of the chosen realization of $G$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: If $d=q$, then $I_{\mathrm{eff}}=I$ is positive definite. If $d>q$, $I_{\eta\eta}$ is a positive-definite principal block. For nonzero $v\in\mathbb R^q$, evaluate the quadratic form of $I$ at $(v,-I_{\eta\eta}^{-1}I_{\eta\psi}v)$; the result is $v^TI_{\mathrm{eff}}v>0$, so $I_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is positive definite in either case. Normalizing $p_{\theta_0+h}$ in the QMD expansion [F1], write $\sqrt{p_{\theta_0+h}}=\sqrt{p_{\theta_0}}+ \tfrac12h^Ts_{\theta_0}\sqrt{p_{\theta_0}}+e_h$ with $\|e_h\|_{L^2(\mu)}=o(\|h\|)$. Expanding the squared norm, whose value is $\int p_{\theta_0+h}d\mu=1$, gives $h^T\mathbb E_{\theta_0}s_{\theta_0}+O(\|h\|^2)+o(\|h\|)=0$. Taking $h=te_j$ and dividing by $t$ proves each score coordinate has mean zero. Since $s_{\theta_0}$ is square integrable by [F1], the iid CLT [F7] gives $\Delta_n\Rightarrow N_d(0,I)$ under AC. Define $r_n=\Delta_{\psi,n}-I_{\psi\eta}I_{\eta\eta}^{-1}\Delta_{\eta,n}$. Its covariance, by block multiplication, is $$\operatorname{Var}(r_n)=I_{\psi\psi}-I_{\psi\eta}I_{\eta\eta}^{-1}I_{\eta\psi}-I_{\psi\eta}I_{\eta\eta}^{-1}I_{\eta\psi}+I_{\psi\eta}I_{\eta\eta}^{-1}I_{\eta\eta}I_{\eta\eta}^{-1}I_{\eta\psi}=I_{\mathrm{eff}}.$$ Thus the linear-map case of Slutsky [F6] gives $r_n\Rightarrow N_q(0,I_{\mathrm{eff}})$; its covariance is the block calculation above.

By [F3], the full MLE satisfies $\sqrt n(\hat\theta_n-\theta_0)=I^{-1}\Delta_n+o_P(1)$. Solving the block system $I(a,b)^T=(\Delta_{\psi,n},\Delta_{\eta,n})^T$ shows its tested block is $a=I_{\mathrm{eff}}^{-1}r_n$, including the empty-nuisance case. If $d=q$, the local null contains only $\theta_0$, so consistency makes the constrained MLE equal to $\theta_0$ with probability tending to one and there is no nuisance expansion to prove. Otherwise, [F3] makes the constrained root-$n$ error bounded. In local coordinates $h=(u,v)$ for $(\eta,\psi)$, the limiting quadratic log likelihood is $Q_n(u,v)=u^T\Delta_{\eta,n}+v^T\Delta_{\psi,n} -\tfrac12\{u^TI_{\eta\eta}u+2u^TI_{\eta\psi}v+v^TI_{\psi\psi}v\}.$ For general $v$, completing the square in $u$ gives the unique maximizer $u=I_{\eta\eta}^{-1}(\Delta_{\eta,n}-I_{\eta\psi}v)$ and the profile $v^Tr_n-\tfrac12v^TI_{\mathrm{eff}}v$ up to a term independent of $v$. At the null $v=0$ this gives the unique nuisance maximizer $u_0=I_{\eta\eta}^{-1}\Delta_{\eta,n}$. On every distance-$\varepsilon$ set from $u_0$, strict positive definiteness of $I_{\eta\eta}$ makes the quadratic log likelihood at least $\tfrac12\lambda_{\min}(I_{\eta\eta})\varepsilon^2$ below its maximum. Uniformity of the likelihood expansion [A1], constrained root-$n$ tightness [F3], and this gap therefore give $\sqrt n(\tilde\eta_n-\eta_0)=I_{\eta\eta}^{-1}\Delta_{\eta,n}+o_P(1)$.

The upper-left block of $I^{-1}$ is $I_{\mathrm{eff}}^{-1}$ by solving the block system $I(x,y)^T=(a,0)^T$. The differentiable local chart has tested coordinate $\psi$, so the Wald statistic in [F2], the expansion in step 2.1, and covariance consistency give $W_n=(I_{\mathrm{eff}}^{-1}r_n)^TI_{\mathrm{eff}} (I_{\mathrm{eff}}^{-1}r_n)+o_P(1) =r_n^TI_{\mathrm{eff}}^{-1}r_n+o_P(1).$

If $d=q$, the nuisance score is empty and the score expansion [A1] at $h=0$ gives $U_{\mathrm{eff},n}=U_{\psi,n}(\theta_0)=\Delta_n+o_P(1)=r_n+o_P(1)$. If $d>q$, the score expansion [A1] at the constrained MLE and $\sqrt n(\tilde\eta_n-\eta_0)=I_{\eta\eta}^{-1}\Delta_{\eta,n}+o_P(1)$ give $U_{\psi,n}(\tilde\theta_n)=r_n+o_P(1)$ and $U_{\eta,n}(\tilde\theta_n)=o_P(1)$. The estimated projection coefficient is bounded in probability by consistency, so the efficient score in [F2] is $r_n+o_P(1)$. Efficient-information consistency and [F5] imply $S_n=r_n^TI_{\mathrm{eff}}^{-1}r_n+o_P(1)$.

The likelihood expansion in [A1] makes $L_n$ equal, up to $o_P(1)$, twice the maximum of $Q_n(u,v)$ over all local $(u,v)$ minus twice its maximum over the null $v=0$. The unrestricted and restricted quadratic maximizers are linear functions of $\Delta_n$, hence are $O_P(1)$ by step 1.1 and [F5]. Taking a bounded local ball large enough with probability arbitrarily close to one justifies using the uniform expansions for both maxima. The profile formula in step 2.1 reduces this difference to $2\sup_v\{v^Tr_n-\tfrac12v^TI_{\mathrm{eff}}v\} =r_n^TI_{\mathrm{eff}}^{-1}r_n.$ The identity follows by completing the square at $v=I_{\mathrm{eff}}^{-1}r_n$. Hence $L_n=r_n^TI_{\mathrm{eff}}^{-1}r_n+o_P(1)$.

Since $r_n\Rightarrow N_q(0,I_{\mathrm{eff}})$ and $I_{\mathrm{eff}}$ is positive definite, its transformed vector $I_{\mathrm{eff}}^{-1/2}r_n$ converges to $N_q(0,I_q)$. The squared Euclidean norm of that limit is $\chi_q^2$ by [F9]. Combining this with steps 3.1–3.3 and [F4]–[F5] proves all three limits and their common first-order approximation. AC is used only through the CLT and normal-law suppliers [F7]–[F8] and the law definition [F9].

specified dominated model, with $\theta_0=(0,\eta_0)$ an interior point of
the full open parameter set $\Theta\subset\mathbb R^q\times\mathbb R^{d-q}$.

null set is a linear subspace of codimension $q\ge1$; all score and
information coordinates below use this chart. Assume QMD at
$\theta_0$ with positive-definite information
$$

$$
and write $I_{\mathrm{eff}}=I_{\psi\psi}-
I_{\psi\eta}I_{\eta\eta}^{-1}I_{\eta\psi}$. If $d=q$, interpret nuisance
blocks as empty, so $I_{\mathrm{eff}}=I_{\psi\psi}=I$ and products involving

localization conclusion. For every finite $M$ the

$$

$$
n^{-1/2}\nabla\ell_n(\theta_0+h/\sqrt n) =\Delta_n-Ih+o_P(1).

and set $T_n=r_n^TI_{\mathrm{eff}}^{-1}r_n$. Then, under the null,
$$
W_n=T_n+o_P(1),\quad S_n=T_n+o_P(1),\quad L_n=T_n+o_P(1),\qquad W_n\Rightarrow\chi_q^2,\quad S_n\Rightarrow\chi_q^2,\quad L_n\Rightarrow\chi_q^2.

derivations.claim: By [F1], there is a common random quadratic form $T_n$ with $W_n=T_n+o_P(1)$, $S_n=T_n+o_P(1)$, and $L_n=T_n+o_P(1)$. Subtracting the first two equalities and applying the triangle inequality gives $W_n-S_n=o_P(1)$; subtracting the second and third gives $S_n-L_n=o_P(1)$; subtracting the third and first gives $L_n-W_n=o_P(1)$.

Theorem [F1] states $T_n\Rightarrow\chi_q^2$ and each statistic has that same limit under the theorem's hypotheses. The differences proved in step 1.1 therefore express first-order equivalence, not exact finite-sample equality.

citations.quote: Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By [[lem-normal-density-has-total-mass-one]] and [[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]], gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. [[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]] makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in [[def-dirac-measure]].

Assume AC. If $X$ has law $N(m,\sigma^2)$ with $\sigma\ge0$, then $\varphi_X(t)=\exp(imt-\sigma^2t^2/2)$ for every real $t$. Moreover $\mathbb EX=m$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X)=\sigma^2$, including $\sigma=0$.

For real $a,b,t$, $\varphi_{aX+b}(t)=e^{itb}\varphi_X(at)$. For a finite mutually independent family $(X_j)_{j=1}^n$ of real random variables, $\varphi_{\sum_jX_j}(t)=\prod_j\varphi_{X_j}(t)$. The empty sum has characteristic function one.

Assume AC. Two Borel probability laws on $\mathbb R$ with equal characteristic functions are equal. In particular a real random variable has a real-valued characteristic function if and only if its law is symmetric under $x\mapsto-x$.

Let $\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be a parametric
model, let $\Theta$ be open in $\mathbb R^d$, and let a supplied sigma-finite
measure $\mu$ dominate every $P_\theta$
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]], [[def-dominated-statistical-experiment]]).
Supply as part of the setup a family of nonnegative finite-valued measurable
functions $p_\theta:\mathcal X\to[0,\infty)$ satisfying
$P_\theta(A)=\int_Ap_\theta\,d\mu$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$
([[def-measure-with-density]]). Thus each $p_\theta$ integrates to one.
The density family is supplied, rather than selected from domination alone;
no choice principle, joint measurability in $(\theta,x)$, or common
exceptional null set is asserted. A supplied extended-valued probability
density can be made finite-valued by setting it to zero on its measurable
infinite-value set, which has measure zero because its integral is one.
The QMD condition is unchanged by replacing any supplied density by an
almost-everywhere equal version: for each fixed $h$, the norm in the
condition below changes only on the union of two null sets.
At an interior point $\theta_0$, the model is
**quadratic-mean differentiable (QMD)** with score $s_{\theta_0}$ if
$s_{\theta_0}:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^d$ is measurable,
$\mathbb E_{\theta_0}\|s_{\theta_0}(X)\|^2<\infty$, and
$$
\int\left(\sqrt{p_{\theta_0+h}}-\sqrt{p_{\theta_0}}- \tfrac12 h^Ts_{\theta_0}\sqrt{p_{\theta_0}}\right)^2d\mu=o(\|h\|^2)
$$
as $h\to0$ with $\theta_0+h\in\Theta$. Values of the score on
$\{p_{\theta_0}=0\}$ do not affect this condition. The Fisher information
associated with this QMD score is
$I_{\theta_0}=\mathbb E_{\theta_0}[s_{\theta_0}s_{\theta_0}^T]$; it may be
singular. QMD is an $L^2(\mu)$ condition and does not assert pointwise
differentiability of $p_\theta$ or local mutual absolute continuity of
$P_\theta$ and $P_{\theta_0}$.

differentiable everywhere with $G'$ not integrable — then the left-hand side does

integrable $f$ need not be the derivative of anything

companion page.

the theorem evaluates $\int_a^b f$ for every integrable derivative, not only for
continuous integrands.

> ([[def-choice-function]]).

there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by

$$\int g\,d(f\,d\mu)=\int gf\,d\mu.$$

compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

bounded and Riemann integrable. Then $f$ is Lebesgue measurable on $[a,b]$ and
is integrable there, and its Lebesgue integral equals its Riemann integral:
$$\int_{[a,b]} f\,d\lambda_1=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx.$$

This is the point at which the completeness of Lebesgue measure is used
essentially: the proof obtains a Borel function equal to $f$ almost everywhere,
and measurability of $f$ itself is then a completeness statement.

translation invariant.

derivations.claim: Put $q_\mu(x)=(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-1/4}e^{-(x-\mu)^2/(4\sigma^2)}$. Direct differentiation gives $q'_\mu=(x-\mu)q_\mu/(2\sigma^2)$ and $q''_\mu=((x-\mu)^2/(4\sigma^4)-1/(2\sigma^2))q_\mu$. Its square is a polynomial times $p_\mu=q_\mu^2$. By [F11] and [F12], $\int (x-\mu)^2p_\mu\,dx=\sigma^2$ and $\int (x-\mu)^4p_\mu\,dx=3\sigma^4$, so $\|q''_\mu\|_2^2=3/(16\sigma^4)<\infty$. Also $s_\mu=2q'_\mu/q_\mu=(x-\mu)/\sigma^2$ has second moment $1/\sigma^2$. The identity $q''_a(x)=q''_0(x-a)$ and [F15] give the same norm for every real shift $a$. The two-variable functions $(x,v)\mapsto q''_{\mu+v}(x)$ and $(x,u)\mapsto q'_{\mu+u}(x)-q'_\mu(x)$ are continuous. To verify the needed product measurability locally, the rectangles $(a,b)\times(c,d)$ with rational endpoints form a countable base of $\mathbb R^2$: inside any open ball about a point, density of the rationals gives a rational rectangle containing that point and contained in the ball. Every open subset is therefore the union of the subfamily of these rectangles contained in it, hence a countable union of measurable product rectangles. Thus preimages of open subsets under these continuous functions belong to $\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$, and also to the product of the Lebesgue sigma-algebras. Their squares and restrictions to compact parameter intervals are consequently product measurable, as required by Tonelli below.

For fixed $x$, the functions $v\mapsto q''_{\mu+v}(x)$ and $u\mapsto q'_{\mu+u}(x)-q'_\mu(x)$ are continuous on each compact interval. By [F13] they are Riemann integrable, by [F9] their integrals are respectively $q'_{\mu+u}(x)-q'_\mu(x)$ and $q_{\mu+t}(x)-q_\mu(x)-tq'_\mu(x)$, and [F14] identifies these with their Lebesgue integrals under the assumed AC. Reversed endpoints give the same identities for negative $u,t$.

Cauchy–Schwarz [F7] on the interval between $0$ and $u$, then Tonelli [F8] and step 1.1, gives $\|q'_{\mu+u}-q'_\mu\|_2^2\le u^2\|q''_0\|_2^2$. The second identity of step 2.1 and another Cauchy–Schwarz/Tonelli application give $\|q_{\mu+t}-q_\mu-tq'_\mu\|_2^2\le |t|\int_0^{|t|}u^2\|q''_0\|_2^2du=|t|^4\|q''_0\|_2^2/3=o(t^2)$. Let $a < b$ be reals and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[a,b]$
([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $f$ is bounded ([[def-bounded-set]]) and Riemann
integrable on $[a,b]$ ([[def-darboux-integral]]).

**The proof gives more than integrability: it gives a partition that works.** For
every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the uniform partition into $N$ parts already
satisfies $U(f,P) - L(f,P) < \varepsilon$, as soon as $N$ is large enough that
$(b-a)/\iota(N)$ is below the $\delta$ that uniform continuity supplies for
$\varepsilon/\bigl(2(b-a)\bigr)$. Uniform continuity is exactly what makes one
$\delta$ serve all $N$ subintervals at once, and it is the only place where the
compactness of $[a,b]$ is used.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $a<b$ and let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ be
bounded and Riemann integrable. Then $f$ is Lebesgue measurable on $[a,b]$ and
is integrable there, and its Lebesgue integral equals its Riemann integral:
$$\int_{[a,b]} f\,d\lambda_1=\int_a^b f(x)\,dx.$$

This is the point at which the completeness of Lebesgue measure is used
essentially: the proof obtains a Borel function equal to $f$ almost everywhere,
and measurability of $f$ itself is then a completeness statement.

Let $n \ge 1$, let $h \in \mathbb{R}^n$, and let $E + h$ be the translate of
$E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-translation-of-a-set-in-rn]]). Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(E+h) = \lambda_n^*(E)$ for **every** subset $E$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $E+h$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(E+h) = \lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

**No choice principle is used.** Lebesgue outer measure is defined as an infimum
and the Carathéodory condition is a family of equations between its values, so
all three clauses are statements about objects that exist in ZF; countable
choice is needed to know that $\lambda_n$ is a measure, not to know that it is
translation invariant.

derivations.claim: Put $q_\mu(x)=(2\pi\sigma^2)^{-1/4}e^{-(x-\mu)^2/(4\sigma^2)}$. Also $s_\mu=2q'_\mu/q_\mu=(x-\mu)/\sigma^2$ has second moment $1/\sigma^2$. The identity $q''_a(x)=q''_0(x-a)$ and [F15] give the same norm for every real shift $a$. The two-variable functions $(x,v)\mapsto q''_{\mu+v}(x)$ and $(x,u)\mapsto q'_{\mu+u}(x)-q'_\mu(x)$ are continuous. To verify the needed product measurability locally, the rectangles $(a,b)\times(c,d)$ with rational endpoints form a countable base of $\mathbb R^2$: inside any open ball about a point, density of the rationals gives a rational rectangle containing that point and contained in the ball. Every open subset is therefore the union of the subfamily of these rectangles contained in it, hence a countable union of measurable product rectangles. Thus preimages of open subsets under these continuous functions belong to $\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$, and also to the product of the Lebesgue sigma-algebras. Their squares and restrictions to compact parameter intervals are consequently product measurable, as required by Tonelli below.

The log likelihood is a constant minus $(2\sigma^2)^{-1}\sum_i(X_i-\mu)^2$. Completing the square shows that the unrestricted MLE is $\hat\mu=\bar X$ and the constrained MLE is $\tilde\mu=\min(0,\bar X)$: when $\bar X\le0$ the unrestricted maximum is feasible, and when $\bar X>0$ the closest feasible point is $0$.

For fixed $x$, the functions $v\mapsto q''_{\mu+v}(x)$ and $u\mapsto q'_{\mu+u}(x)-q'_\mu(x)$ are continuous on each compact interval. By [F13] they are Riemann integrable, by [F10] their integrals are respectively $q'_{\mu+u}(x)-q'_\mu(x)$ and $q_{\mu+t}(x)-q_\mu(x)-tq'_\mu(x)$, and [F14] identifies these with their Lebesgue integrals under the assumed AC. Reversed endpoints give the same identities for negative $u,t$.

Substituting these maximizers into [F1] gives $$L_n=2\{\ell_n(\hat\mu)-\ell_n(\tilde\mu)\}=\frac{n(\bar X_+)^2}{\sigma^2},\qquad \bar X_+=\max(\bar X,0).$$ This follows from $\sum_i(X_i-\mu)^2=\sum_i(X_i-\bar X)^2+n(\mu-\bar X)^2$: the difference is zero for $\bar X\le0$, and otherwise it is $n\bar X^2/\sigma^2$ after multiplication by $2$.

Cauchy–Schwarz [F8] on the interval between $0$ and $u$, then Tonelli [F9] and step 1.1, gives $\|q'_{\mu+u}-q'_\mu\|_2^2\le u^2\|q''_0\|_2^2$. Let $\mathsf P:\Theta\to\mathcal P(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be a parametric
model, let $\Theta$ be open in $\mathbb R^d$, and let a supplied sigma-finite
measure $\mu$ dominate every $P_\theta$
([[def-parametric-statistical-model]], [[def-dominated-statistical-experiment]]).
Supply as part of the setup a family of nonnegative finite-valued measurable
functions $p_\theta:\mathcal X\to[0,\infty)$ satisfying
$P_\theta(A)=\int_Ap_\theta\,d\mu$ for every $A\in\mathcal A$
([[def-measure-with-density]]). Thus each $p_\theta$ integrates to one.
The density family is supplied, rather than selected from domination alone;
no choice principle, joint measurability in $(\theta,x)$, or common
exceptional null set is asserted. A supplied extended-valued probability
density can be made finite-valued by setting it to zero on its measurable
infinite-value set, which has measure zero because its integral is one.
The QMD condition is unchanged by replacing any supplied density by an
almost-everywhere equal version: for each fixed $h$, the norm in the
condition below changes only on the union of two null sets.
At an interior point $\theta_0$, the model is
**quadratic-mean differentiable (QMD)** with score $s_{\theta_0}$ if
$s_{\theta_0}:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R^d$ is measurable,
$\mathbb E_{\theta_0}\|s_{\theta_0}(X)\|^2<\infty$, and
$$
\int\left(\sqrt{p_{\theta_0+h}}-\sqrt{p_{\theta_0}}- \tfrac12 h^Ts_{\theta_0}\sqrt{p_{\theta_0}}\right)^2d\mu=o(\|h\|^2)
$$
as $h\to0$ with $\theta_0+h\in\Theta$. Values of the score on
$\{p_{\theta_0}=0\}$ do not affect this condition. The Fisher information
associated with this QMD score is
$I_{\theta_0}=\mathbb E_{\theta_0}[s_{\theta_0}s_{\theta_0}^T]$; it may be
singular. QMD is an $L^2(\mu)$ condition and does not assert pointwise
differentiability of $p_\theta$ or local mutual absolute continuity of
$P_\theta$ and $P_{\theta_0}$.

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int g\,d(f\,d\mu)=\int gf\,d\mu.$$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$
